introduction-the-amnesiac-database.core: Typical databases store current state and overwrite history: an account balance of €70 doesn't show how it got there. Event sourcing stores the sequence of state-changing events as the source of truth and derives current state by replaying them. CQRS separates the write model (commands, invariants) from read models optimised for queries, often fed by those events.

first_principles.problem: An audit asks why a customer's balance changed last March, and the database only holds today's value.
truths: Reads and writes have different shapes.

analogy.title: A bank statement versus a balance display
analogy.story: The statement lists every transaction; the balance is just the sum.
analogy.breaks: Statements are printed monthly; event stores are appended in real time and replayed by code.

example.title: Account history
example.outcome: history as the source of truth.

check.q: What is the source of truth in event sourcing?
check.a: The append-only sequence of events, not the current state.

cqrs-splitting-the-brain.core: Command Query Responsibility Segregation uses different models for updates and reads. Commands validate business rules against a write model (often an aggregate) and emit changes; queries hit read models (denormalised tables, search indexes, caches) shaped for each screen. Read models update asynchronously, so reads are eventually consistent, but each side scales and evolves independently.

first_principles.problem: One normalised schema serves both complex transactional writes and dozens of dashboard queries, satisfying neither.
truths: Writes need invariants; reads need speed.
derivation: **Project** events or CDC into read stores.
Use CQRS **only where complexity justifies it**.

analogy.title: A restaurant kitchen and its menu board
analogy.story: The kitchen enforces recipes; the menu board is a separate, simplified view updated after changes.
analogy.breaks: Menu boards change rarely; read models update continuously.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Fast reads without compromising write rules.

check.q: What consistency do CQRS read models typically have?
check.a: Eventual consistency, since they're updated asynchronously from the write side.

the-mechanics-of-event-sourcing.core: Each aggregate has an event stream. To handle a command: load events (or snapshot + later events), rebuild state, validate, append new events with an expected version (optimistic concurrency) and publish them. Projections subscribe to build read models. Snapshots speed up long streams, and upcasters handle schema evolution of old events.

first_principles.problem: Two concurrent commands on the same aggregate both append events and violate an invariant.
truths: State is a fold over events.

analogy.title: A ledger where new entries must reference the last line number
analogy.story: If someone added a line meanwhile, you recheck before writing.
analogy.breaks: Ledgers are single-copy; event stores replicate and serve many readers.

check.q: How does event sourcing handle concurrent writes to one aggregate?
check.a: With optimistic concurrency: appends specify an expected stream version and fail if it changed.

the-superpower-time-travel-debugging.core: Because every change is stored, you can reconstruct state at any past moment, replay production events into a fixed version of the code, build new read models retroactively from history, and audit exactly who did what and when. That makes debugging, compliance and analytics dramatically easier.

first_principles.problem: A pricing bug corrupted order totals for two weeks, and the team needs to know exactly which orders and why.

analogy.title: A flight data recorder
analogy.story: After an incident you replay every input to see exactly what happened.
analogy.breaks: Recorders keep hours of data; event stores keep years, which has storage and privacy implications.

example.title: Fixing a projection bug
flow: Corrected totals; list of affected orders produced

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Data repaired from source of truth.

check.q: How does event sourcing help fix a buggy read model?
check.a: Fix the projection code and rebuild the read model by replaying the stored events.

when-not-to-use-event-sourcing.core: Event sourcing adds significant complexity: eventual consistency between writes and reads, event schema evolution forever, replay and snapshot management, harder ad-hoc queries, GDPR deletion challenges (crypto-shredding) and a steep learning curve. Avoid it for simple CRUD domains, small teams, or where an audit table or CDC stream would suffice.

first_principles.problem: A team event-sources a simple settings page and spends months on projections and upcasters.
truths: Events are hard to change once stored.
Simpler patterns often meet audit needs.
derivation: Use for **complex domains** with rich behaviour and audit needs.
Consider **audit logs, temporal tables, CDC** instead.

analogy.title: Keeping a detailed diary of every glass of water
analogy.story: Useful for a medical study, silly for everyday life.
analogy.breaks: Diaries can be thrown away; events are meant to be permanent.

example.title: Decision
flow: Trading ledger with regulatory audit → event sourcing
User preferences page → plain CRUD + audit log

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Use the heavy tool only where it pays.

check.q: Name a simpler alternative to event sourcing for audit needs.
check.a: An audit log table, temporal tables or a CDC stream.
